summary: Kanohar makes electrical equipment such as transformers and helps build the substations and connections used to move electricity to where it is needed.
description: Electricity travels from a generating plant through a network before reaching a railway, factory or home. Different stages need different voltages; voltage is often compared to electrical pressure. A transformer changes the voltage. Kanohar supplies this equipment and also carries out parts of the work needed to build the network.
money: Customers pay for equipment or an agreed construction project. Kanohar pays for metals and other parts, engineers, factory workers, testing, delivery and any site work it has promised. Materials or equipment can need funding before a customer accepts the work and pays.
customers: Electricity utilities, railway and infrastructure organisations, factories and project contractors. They buy specified equipment or a defined project; they do not simply pay Kanohar a household electricity bill.
drivers: Firm customer orders, suitable designs, available materials, reliable manufacturing and testing, ready sites and timely customer payment.

groups.title: Transformers for electricity networks
groups.explanation: A transformer helps change voltage for moving electricity over the network or supplying users. For example, a utility may need equipment at a substation before electricity continues towards customers. The equipment changes voltage; it does not generate the electricity.

groups.title: Equipment for railway power
groups.explanation: Traction means the power used to move trains. These transformer designs meet particular railway supply needs. The buyer specifies what the equipment must do and how it will be checked; making a standard household electrical product is a different job.

groups.title: Equipment at substations
groups.examples: Shunt reactors, gas-insulated switchgear and related substation systems.
groups.explanation: A substation is a place where electricity is connected, controlled or changed to the required voltage. Switchgear turns connections on or off and helps protect equipment; gas-insulated switchgear packs this equipment inside sealed metal enclosures filled with an insulating gas, so it needs less space. A shunt reactor helps control voltage conditions on the network. These are different jobs within the same electricity system.

groups.title: Building parts of the network
groups.explanation: The customer may ask Kanohar to arrange design, equipment purchases and construction, rather than buy a transformer alone. This combined responsibility is called engineering, procurement and construction, often shortened to EPC.

basics.title: Selling equipment differs from delivering a whole project
basics.text: An equipment order may cover making, testing and supplying a transformer. A broader project can also require foundations, other suppliers, site installation and checks before use. Read exactly which jobs the company has agreed to do.

basics.title: The buyer’s approval is part of the sale
basics.text: The customer can require a design to be approved and equipment to pass tests. A completed unit waiting for inspection or installation may still need more work before it can be accepted and paid for.

steps.title: Agree what the customer needs
steps.text: Confirm the design, quantity, price, testing, delivery dates and payment terms.

steps.title: Buy parts and make the equipment
steps.text: Arrange metals and components, then carry out factory work and the required tests.

steps.title: Deliver and complete any site work
steps.text: Send equipment to the customer and do any agreed installation, construction or checks.

steps.title: Obtain acceptance, bill and collect
steps.text: Meet the payment conditions and collect the customer’s money. Some payment may be held back until later checks or defect conditions have been satisfied.

specifics.title: The right type of factory capacity matters
specifics.text: A factory that can make one kind of equipment is not automatically approved for every customer or application. Check what products it can actually make, test and deliver to accepted standards.

specifics.title: A metal-price change can affect the order
specifics.text: Transformers use materials such as copper and electrical steel. If their cost rises after a price is agreed, the contract determines whether the buyer pays more or the company bears the increase.

specifics.title: A shared project is not entirely Kanohar’s sale
specifics.text: Some work is carried out with another participant through a joint operation. Responsibilities and shares of work are agreed between them. The full project value is not automatically the amount belonging to Kanohar.

watch: Which announced opportunities have become firm orders?
A plan to build a power line is different from a purchase contract.
Read the customer, work required, delivery dates and payment terms. Separate equipment-only orders from projects with construction responsibilities, and possible bids from orders already agreed.
Are products being made, accepted and delivered?
A factory opening or finished unit alone does not prove a completed sale.
Read actual output with testing, dispatch and customer acceptance. Check whether units are waiting for inspections or for the site to be ready, and whether that delay ties up materials and money.
Who pays if materials or site work become dearer?
An agreed selling price can leave less profit when costs rise.

Read whether the customer price changes with metal costs and who bears construction delays. Compare the type of work in new orders with earlier work rather than assuming every contract leaves the same profit.
The company may buy materials and pay staff well before the buyer pays.

Look at unpaid customer amounts, stock and cash from operating the business. Check advances paid by buyers and retention, meaning money held back until contract conditions are met, when assessing collection.
Repairs, guarantees and shared projects can still require money.

Read promised warranties, financial guarantees and joint-operation notes. Check what Kanohar itself must supply or fund, and what belongs to another participant, before attributing an entire project to the company.
risks: A few major orders or customers can make production and payments uneven.
Dearer metals, supplier problems, failed tests or site delays can reduce what remains from an order.
Materials, finished equipment and unpaid customer bills can require extra funding.
Defects, promised repairs, guarantees and contract disputes can add costs after supply.
context: Listed in September 2026; quarterly reports have only just started

Kanohar’s shares began trading on 16 September 2026. Its offer combined new shares issued by the company, whose money goes to Kanohar, with existing shares sold by current owners, whose money goes to those sellers. Being listed also means it now publishes results every three months. The first, for April to June 2026, was approved on 6 October 2026, and the company itself notes that some earlier comparison quarters were not reviewed by its auditor. With so few published quarters, a single three-month period can mislead: transformer orders are large and uneven, so check deliveries and payments over several periods.
quiz: If a utility announces a new power line, has Kanohar already earned its value?
No. Kanohar needs an order for its own equipment or work, must meet the agreed conditions and then collect payment. The whole network project does not automatically belong to one supplier.

financialNotes.title: Do not turn the catalogue into a financial split
financialNotes.text: The existing verified snapshot reports company-level revenue and profit on the audited statement’s basis, including its described joint-operation scope. It does not establish separate transformer, reactor or EPC earnings.

financialNotes.title: Compare matching accounting boundaries
financialNotes.text: Read the joint-operation policy, equipment and project revenue recognition and cash-flow statement with the totals. Contract value, backlog, customer advances, recognised sales and profit are different measures and must not be added together.
